title: The Inns of the Silk Road
subtitle: How the caravanserai sheltered merchants, animals and ideas for close to a thousand years

paragraphs.text: For most of recorded history, long-distance trade across Asia moved at the pace of a walking camel. A heavily laden caravan might cover between 30 and 40 kilometres a day, and at the end of each day's march its merchants, drivers and animals needed water, food and, above all, protection from bandits and the weather. The answer that emerged across Persia, Central Asia, Anatolia and the Middle East was the caravanserai, a word that combines the Persian *karvan*, meaning a group of travellers, with *sarai*, a palace or enclosed building. Because a caravan had to reach shelter before dark, caravanserais on the busiest routes were typically built about one day's journey apart. Thousands were constructed along the network of routes that has been known as the Silk Road only since the nineteenth century, when a German geographer coined the term, and several hundred still stand today.

The idea of official stopping places is older than the caravanserai itself. The Greek historian Herodotus, writing in the fifth century BCE, described the Royal Road of the Persian Achaemenid Empire, along which stations with lodgings were placed at regular intervals so that royal messengers could change horses and continue without delay. However, these early posts served the state rather than the trader. The caravanserai as a commercial institution reached its fullest development much later, between roughly the eleventh and seventeenth centuries, when rulers recognised that safe roads attracted merchants and that merchants paid taxes.

Despite being spread over thousands of kilometres, caravanserais were remarkably similar in design. Most were square or rectangular, enclosed by thick, high walls with few or no outer windows, so that the building could be defended like a small fort. A single large gateway, tall and wide enough to admit a camel carrying its full load, was the only way in, and it was closed at sunset. Inside lay an open courtyard, often with a well or cistern at its centre. Around the courtyard ran a series of raised rooms and vaulted recesses where travellers slept and stored their goods, while the animals were usually kept in stables along the outer walls or, in colder regions, in covered halls. In the mountains of eastern Anatolia and northern Iran, where winters were severe, some caravanserais were built almost entirely under one roof, with the courtyard reduced to a small central opening.

Life inside was busy and noisy. A caravan arriving in the late afternoon would unload its bales, water its animals and settle into the rooms around the yard. Larger caravanserais employed a keeper, cooks and a blacksmith who could replace a horseshoe or repair a harness, and some contained a small mosque, a bathhouse and shops. In the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, which controlled much of Anatolia in the thirteenth century, travellers could reportedly stay for up to three days without charge, regardless of their religion or origin; the cost was met by charitable endowments known as *waqf*. Elsewhere, guests usually paid for fodder and food, if not always for their rooms. Because merchants from many lands spent their evenings side by side, the caravanserai also functioned as an exchange of information: prices, news of political events, and even religious and scientific ideas passed along the routes in this way.

Building caravanserais was also an expression of political power. The Safavid ruler Shah Abbas I, who governed Persia from 1588 to 1629, is associated with a great wave of construction intended to revive trade through his territory. Popular tradition credits him with 999 caravanserais, a number that historians treat as symbolic rather than literal, but there is no doubt that the period produced many of the finest surviving examples. Those of his reign were built of brick or of local stone, depending on what materials were available nearby.

The decline of the caravanserai was gradual. From the sixteenth century onwards, European ships carrying goods around Africa began to draw part of the trade between Asia and Europe away from the overland routes, although caravans continued to operate within the region for centuries. The decisive blow came with the railways and, later, the motor road in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. A lorry could cover in a day what had taken a caravan more than a week, and it had no need of a courtyard in which to rest. Many caravanserais were abandoned; others were turned into barracks, prisons or warehouses, and some were simply dismantled so that their stone could be reused.

Interest in these buildings has grown considerably in recent decades. In 2023, UNESCO added a group of 54 caravanserais in Iran to its World Heritage List under the collective title of 'The Persian Caravanserai', recognising both their architectural quality and their role in the history of trade. Conservation, however, is expensive, and the buildings are often located far from towns, which makes it difficult to find a sustainable use for them. One solution has been to convert them into hotels, restaurants or cultural centres. In Isfahan, an eighteenth-century caravanserai has operated for decades as a luxury hotel, and several Anatolian examples now host museums and concerts. Critics argue that such conversions can damage original features, but supporters reply that a building which earns money is far more likely to survive than one which stands empty.
